episodes.title: Cut to the Chase! What should investors make of the US mid-term elections?
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
US midterm elections on 3 November are two weeks away, with prediction markets (Polymarket) pointing to a Democratic clean sweep. Standard Chartered argues the near-term market impact is volatility risk, while the medium-term equity impact is likely limited regardless of outcome, making this more a political/geopolitical risk marker than a direct EM rates driver.

**Key points**
- Polymarket gives Democrats a 91% chance of winning the House and 64% of the Senate, which would be a clean sweep; historically the president's party has kept both chambers only twice in 50 years (1978, 2002).
- Driver of the swing: high gasoline prices and inflation tied to the Iran conflict, which have hurt real incomes and pushed US mortgage rates above 7%.
- Even a Democratic sweep leaves the presidential veto and the Senate filibuster (Republicans likely retain at least 40 seats) intact, making major tax, regulation or climate legislation unlikely over the next two years.
- VIX typically peaks about a month before election day and falls afterward; Q3 earnings season (consensus >30% growth, driven by oil/energy and AI/tech) is seen as a bigger near-term market determinant than the election itself.
- Historically, US equities rally after midterms regardless of outcome: S&P 500 +16.2% on average over 12 months, with an opposition clean sweep (the favoured scenario) historically best at +17.2%, versus +15.4% (divided government) and +14.7% (presidents party retains majority).

**FX / rates implications**
- Primary transmission channel for EM is oil: any late-October escalation in the Middle East/Iran conflict ahead of the election could push oil prices higher, a risk factor for oil-importing EM Asia currencies (INR, PHP) versus oil exporters (COP, MXN to a lesser extent).
- Broader risk sentiment/VIX dynamics (peak-before-election, fade-after) are a generic signal for EM carry trades and risk-on flows into EM Asia/LATAM FX.
- Note: episode does not address the Fed, USD/DXY or UST yields directly, so direct EM FX/rates read-through is limited to the oil and risk-sentiment channels.

**Watch list**
- 3 November: US midterm elections and Senate battleground results.
- Q3 earnings season acceleration over the next two weeks, particularly tech/AI monetization commentary and earnings breadth beyond tech.
- Any late-October Middle East/Iran escalation that could spike oil prices into election day.
- Market pricing of less business-friendly policy risk is not expected until late 2027/early 2028.

episodes.title: Why Oracle's debt load could be your problem
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Oracle, a legacy enterprise-software firm turned AI-era data-center builder, has nearly doubled its debt load in two years to $169 billion, making it the fifth-largest investment-grade issuer (second-largest non-financial after Amazon). Its credit profile is deteriorating just as it sits at the center of a circular financing web tying together OpenAI, Nvidia and Meta — a structure credit analysts increasingly compare to pre-Lehman interconnectedness risk.

**Key points**
- Oracle's debt has nearly doubled in two years to $169 billion; the business shifted from high-margin software to capital-intensive data-center build-out.
- OpenAI has committed roughly $300 billion to Oracle over five years for cloud/compute capacity powering ChatGPT, but OpenAI's financials are not public, raising concentration-risk concerns.
- Oracle issued a force-majeure notice to creditors flagging possible delays on loan repayments tied to a New Mexico data center built for OpenAI, while publicly insisting the project is on schedule.
- S&P downgraded Oracle's credit in July; the company now sits just one notch above junk status.
- Oracle's credit default swap (CDS) spreads are rising, signaling the market sees growing default risk even though analysts don't see imminent bankruptcy or a near-term downgrade.
- Circular deal structure: Oracle buys Nvidia chips to build data centers; OpenAI pays Oracle for cloud capacity; Nvidia invests in OpenAI — raising systemic-risk concerns if any link falters.

**FX / rates implications**
- Primarily a US corporate credit story, but a disorderly Oracle credit event (junk downgrade, forced deleveraging) would hit broad risk sentiment, pressuring high-beta EM FX (IDR, INR, PHP, MXN, BRL, ZAR-type currencies) and widening EM credit spreads via contagion from US high-yield/IG credit stress.
- A downgrade to junk would force pension/investment-grade-only funds out of Oracle paper, a precedent that could re-rate perceived risk across AI-linked credit broadly, tightening financial conditions and indirectly supporting USD/DXY on safe-haven flows if it escalates.
- Any AI-bubble unwind narrative (explicitly likened to a Lehman-style event) is a tail risk for global risk appetite, carry trades, and EM capital flows more broadly, though no direct EM Asia/LATAM mechanism is discussed.

**Watch list**
- Oracle CDS spread trends and any further rating agency action (next move below investment grade would be a major credit event).
- Progress/delays on the New Mexico OpenAI data center and any further force-majeure notices.
- Transparency (or lack thereof) around OpenAI's financials ahead of any potential IPO, which could reprice the whole Oracle-Nvidia-OpenAI-Meta credit chain.

episodes.title: Bull Case for Coreweave, Putin Suggests Summit, and the Read on Retail 10/19/26
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A US-equity-focused show (AI stock rebound, CoreWeave, Anthropic/Musk philanthropy, housing) that still carries real macro signal for an EM trader via oil prices, US Treasury yields, and the Russia-Ukraine-driven geopolitical risk backdrop ahead of a proposed Trump-Putin-Xi summit.

**Key points**
- WTI jumped ~1.5% intraday, briefly topping $103/bbl after Trump waived new sanctions/duties on Russia two days before implementation and eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
- Putin is reportedly pushing for a trilateral summit with Trump and Xi (APEC, Shenzhen, Nov 18-19) to end the Ukraine war, excluding Zelensky; Piper Sandler's Michael Cantrowitz argues bond yields are unlikely to fall sustainably unless oil drops sharply, unemployment rises, or another AI-stock risk-off episode hits.
- Nasdaq +1.2%, S&P +0.5% rebound after last week's 4%+ Nasdaq selloff; semis (SOXX) snapped a 9-day, 15% losing streak; CoreWeave got a Goldman upgrade but still slipped intraday on bearish leverage concerns (800% debt/equity, negative working capital).
- Home-builder sentiment hit a 14-year low (29, NAHB) as 30yr mortgage rates rose to 7.4%; Fannie Mae revised 2026 mortgage-rate forecast up to 7.5% from 6.7%.
- 13 Republican senators have opposed the Russia diesel/sanctions deal, signaling domestic political friction around Trump's Russia pivot.

**FX / rates implications**
- Higher-for-longer US rates narrative (oil-driven inflation stickiness, strong labor market) reinforces a firmer USD/UST-yield backdrop that is typically a headwind for EM Asia and LATAM carry trades.
- Elevated/volatile oil prices directly pressure oil-importing EM Asia currencies (INR, PHP, IDR) via terms-of-trade and current-account channels, while supporting commodity-linked LATAM (COP, MXN via energy linkages; watch BRL/CLP less directly).
- Risk-on tape (AI/tech bounce) is modestly supportive of EM risk sentiment and carry, but fragile given last week's selloff and ongoing geopolitical overhang.

**Watch list**
- Proposed Trump-Putin-Xi summit, Nov 18-19 at APEC Shenzhen — outcome could swing oil prices and broader risk sentiment.
- US midterm elections (Nov 3) as a catalyst for shifts in Russia/Ukraine and tariff/sanctions policy.
- Big Tech capex updates this week (SpaceX-related, Meta) and US mortgage-rate trajectory as read-throughs for US rates path.

episodes.title: The Credit Market Lens: Improved Optics But Unchanged Economics in Software Loans
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
This episode is a PIMCO credit-market note on the US leveraged loan software sector, which has underperformed in 2025 on fears that AI will disrupt existing business models. It's a niche single-sector credit piece with limited direct read-through to EM FX/rates, though it offers a window into broader leveraged credit stress and dispersion.

**Key points**
- Software loans are among the worst-performing pockets of the leveraged loan market this year, weighing on the Morningstar LSTA US leveraged loan index given software's >10% weight.
- Spreads tightened over summer (about 100bps inside June wides, retracing roughly one-third of the year's widening) but have widened again since early September.
- Average bid price for software loans remains ~8 points below non-software peers (vs ~10 points in June).
- No causal link seen between the software equity rally and loan spread tightening; large-cap software equities have investment-grade status and cheaper funding access unavailable to leveraged-loan issuers.
- About $62 billion of software loans mature in 2028-2029; liability management exercises (LMEs) are the path of least resistance, with amend-and-extend costs ranging from +25bps to +150bps plus below-par discounts depending on issuer quality.

**FX / rates implications**
- No direct EM FX/rates linkage; this is a US corporate leveraged loan credit story rather than a sovereign or macro driver.
- Relevant mainly as a gauge of US credit market health and dispersion, which can feed into broader risk sentiment and credit spread conditions that occasionally spill into EM risk appetite and capital flows.

**Watch list**
- Further spread moves in software loans as a signal of credit dispersion/risk appetite.
- $62bn of software loan maturities in 2028-2029 and refinancing/LME costs as a barometer of leveraged credit stress.
- Any read-through from AI disruption narratives into broader tech credit and equity risk sentiment.
